summary: Extends the traffic description used by Integrated Services (the TSpec) so a sender of data that can be compressed can hint at how much compression routers might get. Routers can use that hint when deciding how much capacity to reserve. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If you pack a suitcase that can be squished smaller, telling the airline helps them save room for others. This lets a sender tell the network its data can be squished.

questions: what is a compressibility hint in intserv
how does header compression affect rsvp reservations
subtitle: How a sender can tell routers its data will compress on a link, so they do not reserve more capacity than needed.

tldr.problem: Integrated Services routers reserve capacity based on the sender's TSpec, but a router that can compress the flow on a link (for example with IP/UDP/RTP header compression) needs less than the TSpec says, so it might wrongly reject a reservation it could have served.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a compressibility hint to its Sender TSpec: a hint number naming the kind of compression plus an optional compression factor in percent. Routers that can compress use it to compute a smaller 'compressed TSpec'; other routers ignore it.
tldr.outcome: Routers that support the compression can admit flows more accurately. The sender TSpec on the wire is never modified, and routers that do not understand the hint should silently ignore it.

facts.label: Header compression example
facts.value: 40 bytes of IP/UDP/RTP header to 4 bytes

today: RFC 3006 is a Proposed Standard (November 2000), and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on the Integrated Services specifications in RFC 2210 and the header compression in RFC 2508.

sections.title: The Problem with Compressible Flows
sections.content:
In an Integrated Services network, RSVP (RFC 2205) is used to signal resource needs. The sender describes its traffic in a SENDER_TSPEC object, and the routers use that, among other things, for admission control and resource allocation.

The trouble starts when a router can compress the flow on a link. With IP/UDP/RTP header compression (RFC 2508), the bandwidth needed on that interface is less than the TSpec states, so the router might reject a reservation that it could in fact have accommodated. The sender cannot just shrink its TSpec, because it does not know whether the routers on the path can compress. Probably only some of them, such as those on low-speed serial links, will.

The scope is limited to compression done link by link, as with header compression. Cases such as transcoding or audio silence detection, which change the bandwidth at all downstream nodes, are left for further study.
sections.eli5: A bus company reserves seats by counting how many people you say are coming. If your group could fold up small on a short ride, the bus might say no even though there is room. This fixes that.

sections.title: Putting a Hint in the Sender TSpec
sections.content:
The RFC adds a compressibility hint to the Sender TSpec. It gives these reasons: the sender knows best what its data will look like; unlike the Adspec, the Sender TSpec is not modified in transit; and RSVP treats the TSpec as opaque parameters handed to traffic control, so the hint is just another such parameter.

The alternative, a new object in the RSVP PATH message, would require changing RSVP message processing and would not help when something other than RSVP is used to reserve resources.

The hint must say what type of compression is possible (for example IP/UDP/RTP) and give enough information for a router to work out the likely compression ratio. For simple IP/UDP/RTP header compression, saying that the data is IP/UDP/RTP may be enough, together with the maximum packet size and local conditions at the router. Otherwise the sender can add quantitative parameters.
sections.eli5: The sender writes a note on its own ticket saying 'this can be folded up small, like this.' Nobody changes the note on the way, so every stop along the trip can read it.

sections.title: Admission Control with a Compressed TSpec
sections.content:
A router that gets a hint it understands may compute a compressed TSpec and use it in place of the sender's TSpec for admission control and resource allocation. In the RFC's example, the token bucket rate r is 48 kbps, the bucket depth b is 120 bytes, the maximum packet size M is 120 bytes and the minimum policed unit m is 64 bytes. The hint says IP/UDP/RTP with a compression factor of 70%, which comes from compressing 40 bytes of header to 4 bytes on a 120 byte packet. The router scales r and b down to 33.6 kbps and 84 bytes. M becomes 84 bytes, and m becomes 28 bytes because a minimum-size packet saves the same 36 bytes.

In general, with compression factor f percent and N bytes saved per packet, the compressed values are r' = r * f/100, b' = b * f/100, p' = p, M' = M-N and m' = m-N. The subtraction only holds for algorithms that remove a fixed number of bytes, as header compression does. The router may need worst-case assumptions about N, which depends on things like UDP checksums and RTP timestamp linearity.

If the sender is willing to let the router work out the gain itself, it can omit the explicit factor. For several senders sharing one reservation, each sender TSpec is reduced by its own factor and the results are added. For Guaranteed service, the RSpec rate R is scaled by a burst-weighted average factor f_avg, and the hop inflates its C term by dividing it by f_avg/100 so that delay stays what the receiver expected.

Compression is not fully deterministic, so a flow may turn out less compressible than assumed. Any extra traffic is policed under the normal intserv rules for the service. A router that used the hint should police as if it were at the network edge, and services that police on M keep using the uncompressed value.
sections.eli5: If a suitcase will shrink to 70 percent, the airline saves 70 percent of the room. If it does not shrink as much as promised, the extra stuff gets treated like extra luggage.

sections.title: The Extended TSpec Format
sections.content:
The hint rides in the sender TSpec using the encoding rules of Appendix A in RFC 2210. Compared with the RFC 2210 TSpec, the overall length and the length of the service 1 data each grow by 3 words, and a new parameter follows the original ones: parameter 126, Compression_Hint, with a length of 2 words. The Token_Bucket_TSpec stays parameter 127. Like it, the hint is not specific to one service (its number is below 128) and sits in the default/global information, service number 1.

The parameter holds a 32-bit hint, then a 32-bit compression factor f expressed as a percentage. The valid range is (0,100]. The reserved value 0 means the sender does not know or wants routers to decide, and 100 means no compression is expected. More than one hint may appear, by repeating parameter 126, if several compression schemes could apply.

The hint's high-order 16 bits are the IP-compression-protocol number from RFC 1332 and RFC 2509. The low-order 16 bits are a sub-option for cases where the protocol number alone is not enough for int-serv purposes.
sections.eli5: The note has a code for the kind of squishing, like a color-coded sticker, and a number saying how small it gets. A zero means 'you work it out', and 100 means 'it will not shrink.'

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
A router that does not understand the hint should silently ignore it instead of treating the TSpec as malformed. It should behave as if the parameter were absent but leave it intact in the object it forwards. RFC 2210 lets TSpecs with unknown parameters be parsed, but it does not say what to do with unknown objects, so some RSVP implementations may discard PATH messages carrying the hint.

In that case the router should send a PathErr message to the sending host with Error code 21, Sub-code 04 (malformed TSpec). The host may conclude that the hint caused the problem and send a new PATH without it.

The RFC also floats a way to cope with future changes: dividing the parameter space so that numbers of the form x1xxxxxx are ignored if unrecognized and x0xxxxxx cause an error.
sections.eli5: If a stop along the way cannot read the note, it should just pass it along unread. If a stop gets confused and sends it back, the sender can try again without the note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says these extensions pose essentially the same security risks as RFC 2210. A sender who falsely says its data is compressible is equivalent to a sender providing an insufficiently large TSpec, and it is dealt with in the same way. The policing rule in the admission-control section, which polices against the compressed TSpec, is what limits the damage to other reserved flows.
sections.eli5: If someone lies and says their bag will squish when it will not, the extra stuff is simply treated as extra, so nobody else loses their seat.
